answer.question: Which patients are eligible for the hybrid hospital-wide readmission measure?
answer.answer: Under the methodology’s listed criteria, eligible patients are Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries aged 65 or older, discharged alive from a non-federal acute-care hospital, and enrolled in Part A for the 12 months before and including the index admission. The March 2023 supplement says Medicare Advantage admissions were added to the current measure cohort, with the other specifications unchanged. Exclusions include admissions to PPS-exempt cancer hospitals, patients without at least 30 days of post-discharge FFS enrollment, discharges against medical advice, and admissions for primary psychiatric diagnoses, rehabilitation, or medical cancer treatment; cancer patients admitted for other diagnoses or cancer surgery remain eligible. Although the listed criteria say “Not transferred,” transferred patients remain in the measure cohort, and readmission accountability goes to the hospital that ultimately discharges the patient to a non-acute-care setting.

answer.answer: For each of the 10 publicly reported HCAHPS measures, CMS first turns survey responses into a 0–100 linear score by scoring, adjusting, rescaling, averaging across quarters, and rounding. The numerator counts eligible patients who received all applicable interventions: within three hours of presentation, measure an initial lactate level, draw blood cultures before antibiotics, and administer broad-spectrum or other antibiotics; within six hours, repeat the lactate if the initial level is >2 mmol/L. For septic shock, it also includes giving 30 ml/kg crystalloid within three hours for hypotension or lactate = 4 mmol/L, and within six hours applying vasopressors for hypotension unresponsive to initial fluids to maintain MAP = 65 mm Hg, plus reassessing volume status and tissue perfusion when hypotension persists (MAP < 65 mm Hg) after fluids or the initial lactate level = 4 mmol/L. [1][2]
Excluded patients are those without severe sepsis; transferred in from another acute care facility; receiving intravenous antibiotics for more than 24 hours before presentation of severe sepsis; or with comfort or palliative care directives within three hours of severe-sepsis presentation or within six hours of septic-shock presentation. [3][4] Also excluded are patients with an administrative contraindication to care within six hours of presentation of severe sepsis or septic shock, those with septic shock or severe sepsis discharged within six hours of presentation, those with a length of stay longer than 120 days, and those included in a clinical trial. [5][6]

answer.question: Which indicators make up the CMS PSI 90 composite, and how are they combined?
answer.answer: The CMS PSI 90 composite includes PSI 03 pressure ulcer rate; PSI 06 iatrogenic pneumothorax rate; PSI 08 in-hospital fall with hip fracture rate; PSI 09 perioperative hemorrhage or hematoma rate; PSI 10 postoperative acute kidney injury requiring dialysis rate; PSI 11 postoperative respiratory failure rate; PSI 12 perioperative pulmonary embolism or deep vein thrombosis rate; PSI 13 postoperative sepsis rate; PSI 14 postoperative wound dehiscence rate; and PSI 15 unrecognized accidental puncture or laceration rate. It combines these indicators as a weighted average calculated at the hospital level; the excerpt does not give the individual weights. For physician group practices, the measure is calculated at the hospital level and then weighted by the practice’s clinical episode volume at each hospital.

answer.question: What period does the BPCI Advanced version of PSI 90 use, and how does it differ from the published specification?
answer.answer: BPCI Advanced calculates PSI 90 using October 1 through September 30, with the index admission’s discharge date determining the calendar year for the claim. Its version uses a two-year period instead of the three-year period in the published specification.
